Correct that to 'worst-group preference win rate.' A latent component in the method and a group in the evaluation are not interchangeable. The decision cites the measured group-level comparison, not a reported worst-component rate.
Should we credit a particular design feature for the six-point difference?

The decision does not isolate a cause for the difference. It selects ShiftGuard-RLHF on the basis of its observed worst-group result against pooled RLHF at 12,000 labels. Attributing the entire gap to a specific feature would add an explanation that this decision does not state.
Could this comparison tell us how reliable the six-point difference is across individual runs?

Not from the decision statement alone. It gives the reported rates and label count, but no per-run values or uncertainty estimate. You can cite the 6-percentage-point difference without claiming a particular degree of variability or statistical significance.
Would 'statistically significant improvement' be appropriate?

No statistical test or uncertainty interval is included in this decision. The accurate claim is that ShiftGuard-RLHF achieved 60% versus pooled RLHF's 54% worst-group preference wins in the stated comparison.
Does choosing ShiftGuard-RLHF prove that its latent preferences were identified under every shift?

No. The selection rests on a worst-group performance comparison at 12,000 labels. That performance measure is distinct from a claim that latent preferences were identifiable under every adaptive shift or that annotation noise was fully separated from them.
Can I leave the baseline out and say 'select ShiftGuard-RLHF because it reached 60%'?

That would omit an important part of the stated reason. The decision is motivated by 60% *versus pooled RLHF's 54%* at 12,000 labels. Including the baseline makes clear what the reported performance was compared against.
Is pooled RLHF the method we're selecting?
No. ShiftGuard-RLHF is the selected method for adaptive shifts. Pooled RLHF is the comparison baseline whose reported worst-group win rate was 54% in the 12,000-label setting.
What if I phrase the decision as 'ShiftGuard-RLHF replaces pooled RLHF everywhere'?

That would extend its scope beyond adaptive shifts and beyond the reported comparison. The decision selects ShiftGuard-RLHF for adaptive shifts because of the 60%-versus-54% worst-group result at 12,000 labels. It does not make a universal replacement claim.
Could 'for adaptive shifts' be understood as a claim that the policy never changes again?

No. It names the setting of the choice: policy adaptation can induce changes in the distribution encountered. It should not be turned into an assertion about a fixed policy or a guarantee about the pattern of future changes.
Does the difference of six percentage points depend on which method's worst group we use?

The calculation simply subtracts the reported worst-group rates, 60% and 54%. It does not require claiming that both minima refer to the same underlying group. That distinction is why the result is appropriately stated as a comparison of worst-group rates, not as a measured gain for a particular identified group.
Can we describe the selection as supported by the adaptive evaluation without describing it as a universal theorem?

Yes. The observed 60% versus 54% worst-group comparison at 12,000 labels supports selecting ShiftGuard-RLHF for adaptive shifts. It remains an empirical rationale for that scoped decision, not a proof that one method dominates under all possible shifts.
Give me a version suitable for a decision record, with no extra claims.
Select ShiftGuard-RLHF for adaptive shifts. At 12,000 labels, it achieved a 60% worst-group preference win rate versus 54% for pooled RLHF, a 6-percentage-point difference.

I have another proposal: PanelDRO-RLHF uses pseudonymous cross-policy recontact and randomized repeated comparisons to identify stable dissent, then optimizes pessimistic latent-profile win rates. Can we unpack what that actually proposes?

PanelDRO-RLHF has an identification part and an optimization part. It proposes recontacting participants pseudonymously across policies and using randomized repeated comparisons to distinguish stable dissent from variation in individual annotations. It would then optimize pessimistic win rates for latent preference profiles. That is a proposed method, not a claim that stable dissent has already been identified or that any win rate has been achieved.
What does pseudonymous cross-policy recontact mean here?

It means retaining a way to relate a participant's feedback across different policy settings without using their observed annotator group identity. The cross-policy link is important to the proposal: it could make persistence of a preference assessable as the policy changes. 'Pseudonymous' does not mean that the feedback is entirely unlinkable, and it does not specify how recontact or pseudonyms would be implemented.
So it is different from treating all comparisons as isolated anonymous annotations?

Yes, conceptually. Pseudonymous recontact permits a connection between observations across policies, whereas isolated annotations would not supply that particular connection. The proposal depends on that ability to examine whether dissent persists across changing policy settings. It does not require attaching a named group identity to the person being recontacted.
Does recontact mean we learn who the annotator is?

Not as stated. The proposal says *pseudonymous* recontact, not identification by name or observed group membership. It calls for linking feedback across policy settings while preserving the distinction between a participant-level link and an annotator group label. It does not make a broader guarantee about privacy or specify what other information is available.
Why does the cross-policy part matter rather than repeating comparisons under just one policy?

The goal concerns preferences under policy-induced distribution shifts. Comparing feedback linked across policies could help ask whether a dissenting preference remains stable when policy behavior changes what is encountered. Repetition within one policy may reveal consistency in that setting without addressing persistence across policies. Cross-policy recontact is proposed to bring that additional question into view, not to guarantee that every comparison remains comparable after a shift.
If a person responds differently under two policies, is that automatically noise?

No. The policy settings may present different comparisons or contexts, so a changed response does not, on its own, identify annotation noise. Equally, a consistent response alone does not prove a stable latent preference. The proposal uses recontact and randomized repetition to make the distinction more assessable; the conditions under which it can actually be identified would still need to be specified.
What is meant by randomized repeated comparisons?

The proposal calls for repeated preference comparisons with an element of randomization rather than relying only on a fixed sequence of observations. Repetition can provide information about variability in responses, and randomization can help make the repeated observations more informative for the question being asked. The statement does not specify what is randomized, how often comparisons repeat, or a particular sampling procedure.
Should I say randomization removes all annotation noise?

No. Randomization is part of the proposed observation design, not a mechanism that eliminates noise. The purpose is to help distinguish stable dissent from variability in annotations. Whether it succeeds depends on the observations and the assumptions of an identification argument; the proposal supplies neither a completed proof nor a noise-free dataset.
Does 'repeated comparisons' mean the same person necessarily sees exactly the same pair on every policy?

That is not specified. The proposal names randomized repeated comparisons alongside cross-policy recontact, but gives no rule about which pairs recur or exactly how repetitions are distributed across policies. We can discuss repetition as a way to examine consistency without asserting a particular comparison schedule.
How would you describe stable dissent without assuming that all disagreement is persistent?

Stable dissent is a persistent preference pattern that differs from another preference pattern, rather than an isolated conflicting annotation. The proposal seeks to identify it, not to label every dissenting response as stable. Repeated observations linked across policies could be relevant evidence, but a distinction from annotation noise requires conditions under which those observations genuinely support that interpretation.
Does dissent necessarily mean a minority preference?

Dissent describes a preference that conflicts with another pattern. In the broader objective, protecting conflicting minority preferences is the motivation, but this proposal does not establish the size of any latent profile or declare that every identified dissenting pattern belongs to a minority group. Those are different claims.
Can cross-policy recontact itself prove the preference is stable?

No. It supplies a way to relate feedback across policy settings; the content of that feedback, the comparisons presented, and potential annotation variation still matter. A link between observations is useful for asking about stability, but linking alone is not an identification theorem.
What does 'latent-profile' refer to in the optimization objective?

It refers to modeled preference profiles inferred rather than observed as annotator group identities. Optimizing profile-level win rates is a way to attend to conflicting patterns without assuming one pooled preference represents everyone. A latent profile should not automatically be described as a named group, an individual participant, or a verified minority population.
Why not just optimize a pooled win rate?

A pooled measure can obscure how a conflicting preference pattern fares. PanelDRO-RLHF instead proposes optimizing pessimistic win rates for latent profiles, keeping attention on outcomes that might be poorly served by an aggregate objective. The proposal does not specify a mathematical objective or report that this choice improves evaluated group outcomes.
What is the force of the word 'pessimistic'?

It qualifies the latent-profile win rates used for optimization: the approach is meant to avoid treating favorable estimates as certain when assessing how a profile fares. The proposal does not define a particular lower bound, confidence level, uncertainty set, or algorithm. We should retain the term without inventing its formal implementation.
Does pessimistic mean the objective is the minimum over the profiles?

The proposal says it optimizes *pessimistic latent-profile win rates*, but does not specify the aggregation rule across profiles. It would be too specific to assign a particular minimum or formula as though it were already stated. The core idea is conservative treatment of win rates associated with modeled preference profiles.
Does this require observed group labels at the optimization stage?

No observed group identities are part of the stated proposal. Pseudonymous cross-policy recontact provides a link between observations, and the optimization concerns *latent* profiles. Neither should be silently replaced with group-labeled training or group-labeled policy optimization.
Could the pseudonymous link itself be treated as a latent profile label?

They serve different purposes. A pseudonymous link relates feedback from a participant across policy settings; a latent profile represents a modeled preference pattern. A participant's linked observations might inform a profile model, but the proposal does not say every pseudonym corresponds to a separate profile or that profiles are known from the links alone.
If recontact is possible, does that mean distribution shift stops being a problem?

No. Recontact can help relate responses across changing policies, but the policies may still induce different distributions of comparisons. Linking participants does not guarantee that the observations needed to compare their preferences are present in all settings. The proposal addresses a challenge posed by shift; it does not declare the challenge removed.
Would a high latent-profile win rate be enough to show the worst-group target was met?

No. A latent profile is a modeled preference pattern, whereas the target is a *worst-group preference win rate* improvement of at least 5 percentage points versus pooled RLHF with matching feedback budgets. Profile-level optimization could be relevant to that goal, but the proposal gives no evaluated worst-group comparison and no guarantee that profiles coincide with groups.
And identifying stable dissent is not the same as establishing identifiability conditions?

Correct. The proposal describes an observation design intended to identify stable dissent. Establishing identifiability conditions would require stating when stable preference disagreement and annotation noise are distinguishable under policy-induced distribution shift, and where the observations remain ambiguous. Pseudonymous recontact and randomized repetitions are proposed ingredients, not a completed conditions-and-proof statement.
What if the repeated comparisons are perfectly consistent? Can I declare stable dissent identified?

Consistency would be relevant, but on its own it would not justify that conclusion in every setting. One would still have to establish what the observations can distinguish, especially if policies change which comparisons appear. The proposal does not state that a particular amount of consistency suffices.
Does the proposal specify how many participants to recontact or how many repetitions are required?
No. It does not give a recontact count, repetition count, feedback budget, or threshold for sufficient evidence. Adding any of those as a settled design parameter would extend beyond the proposal.
Does the name PanelDRO-RLHF give us a particular DRO uncertainty set or estimator?

No. PanelDRO-RLHF is the proposed method's name. Its supplied content is pseudonymous cross-policy recontact, randomized repeated comparisons to identify stable dissent, and optimization of pessimistic latent-profile win rates. The name alone does not specify a formal uncertainty set, estimator, or training algorithm.
Could we say the randomization identifies a causal effect of policy changes on dissent?

That would be an added claim. The proposal says randomized *repeated comparisons* are used to identify stable dissent; it does not state that policy assignments are randomized or that a causal effect of policy changes is identified. Keep the proposed identification target focused on stable preference disagreement versus annotation variation.
How would you keep the proposal's purpose and its limits together in one sentence?

PanelDRO-RLHF proposes pseudonymous recontact across policies and randomized repeated comparisons to identify stable dissent, followed by optimization of pessimistic latent-profile preference win rates; it does not yet establish the identifiability conditions or demonstrate a worst-group advantage over pooled RLHF.
Can cross-policy recontact distinguish persistent dissent from session noise when annotator attrition depends on policy outputs?

That is an open identifiability question for PanelDRO-RLHF. Pseudonymous cross-policy recontact can connect an annotator's responses across policies, and randomized repeated comparisons can help examine variation within the feedback obtained. But if whether an annotator returns depends on policy outputs, the responses available after recontact may be selected. The resulting pattern could reflect persistent dissent, session noise, or who remained observable; recontact alone does not distinguish those explanations.
Why does output-dependent attrition matter more than simply having fewer responses?

The concern is not just a smaller quantity of feedback. If the likelihood of a response depends on what the policy outputs, then the observed cross-policy feedback may systematically omit some of the situations or perspectives relevant to the disagreement. An apparent change in dissent could reflect that selection rather than a change in preferences or the amount of session noise. Whether this ambiguity can be resolved is the question, not a finding that it has occurred.
Does the pseudonymous link at least let us identify the people who disappear?

It can, in principle, distinguish a linked participant who has no later response from one who provides feedback again, to the extent the proposed recontact structure records that distinction. It does not reveal what the missing participant would have preferred about the later policy outputs. Nor does a pseudonym disclose an annotator group identity.
Could the responses from the people who do return establish that their dissent is persistent?

They could provide evidence about persistence among those observed across policies, provided the comparisons and noise assumptions support that interpretation. But a conclusion about returning respondents need not extend to those who attrited. Even among returners, repeated disagreement has to be separated from session noise rather than simply labeled persistent.
Is attrition itself evidence that the absent annotators held a minority preference?

No. If attrition depends on policy outputs, that raises a selection concern, but it does not disclose any absent annotator's preference or establish membership in a minority. Inferring persistent dissent merely from a failure to respond would add an unsupported claim.
What exactly is session noise in the question?

It is variation in annotations associated with the session rather than a stable dissenting preference. The question asks whether cross-policy recontact can distinguish that kind of variation from persistent disagreement when the set of observed annotators may change in a way related to policy outputs. It does not specify a noise distribution or say that session noise is the only other explanation for conflicting responses.
Would repeating a comparison within the same session be enough to classify inconsistency as noise?

Not automatically. A repeated comparison can show how responses vary within an observed session, but interpreting that variation as session noise requires assumptions about what remains stable and what the repetition measures. Moreover, within-session repetition cannot directly provide the unobserved responses of annotators who do not return across policies.
And could randomized repetitions solve the attrition problem by themselves?

Randomizing repeated comparisons can make the observed repetition informative for distinguishing stable responses from variation in the sessions that occur. It does not, on its own, randomize who stays available for recontact or make missing feedback observable. If attrition depends on policy outputs, a randomization of comparisons should not be treated as a blanket cure for that selection.
What if the returning participants give the same dissenting response every time?

That would be consistent with persistent dissent among those returning participants, but it would not by itself identify what happened among participants who attrited. It also would not establish, without further conditions, that the observed consistency could not arise under a particular form of session-related variation. The scope of a persistence claim matters.
Could an apparent disappearance of dissent be explained entirely by attrition?

Conceptually, yes: one possible explanation is that participants whose feedback would express dissent do not return in the later observations. Other explanations could also fit an apparent disappearance. The question does not state which explanation applies, so the observation alone would not tell us that dissent ended or that attrition caused its apparent disappearance.
Could dissent appear more common for the same selection reason?

Yes, in principle. If the people observed after a policy change are not representative of those whose preferences one wishes to characterize, the observed frequency of dissent might move in either direction. The direction cannot be inferred just from knowing that attrition depends on policy outputs.
Does output-dependent attrition mean the policy actually changes people's preferences?

No. Attrition concerns which annotations remain available. A policy's outputs might affect the chance that someone responds without telling us whether their underlying preference changed. The question is specifically about separating persistent dissent from session noise in the presence of that observation problem, not about establishing a causal change in preferences.
How does this affect what we mean by identifying stable dissent?

It forces us to specify the population and observations to which identification applies. One might be able to examine a pattern among participants with linked responses, yet lack grounds to infer the same pattern for everyone initially available or for those absent after a shift. Calling dissent 'identified' without that qualification could mistake a selected observed pattern for a persistent preference in the broader setting.
Is a comparison across policy settings still meaningful if only some participants can be recontacted?

It can be meaningful for the linked feedback that is actually observed, but the inference drawn from it must respect the selection of participants and comparisons. Cross-policy linkage supplies continuity for some observations; it does not guarantee that the observed participants and policy outputs provide the information required for a broader persistence claim.
What kind of identifiability condition would the question require, in general terms?

It would need to say when the observed links and repeated comparisons suffice to separate stable dissent from session variation despite output-dependent missing responses. In particular, it would have to address which preferences can be compared across policies, what the repetition reveals about session noise, and how attrition affects the interpretation of the feedback that remains. No such sufficient condition is supplied by the question.
Could we just assume attrition is unrelated to preferences and declare the problem solved?

An explicit assumption might narrow a theoretical claim, but it cannot be silently inserted as an established fact. The question says attrition depends on policy outputs; even if preferences are not directly observed among those who leave, their absence may still limit comparisons involving those outputs. A defensible answer would state any additional assumptions and explain what they do and do not identify.
Does dependence on policy outputs automatically make identification impossible?

That would be too strong. Output-dependent attrition creates a possible ambiguity, but whether it prevents identification depends on what is observed and on justified assumptions about recontact, comparisons, noise, and missingness. The question asks whether the distinction can be made under that complication; it does not announce a universal impossibility result.
Is the important distinction between tracking a participant and having comparable comparisons?

Both matter, but they solve different parts of the problem. A pseudonymous link can relate feedback from the same participant across policies when they respond. Comparable repeated comparisons can help interpret changes or consistency in their responses. Neither supplies feedback from an attrited participant, and neither alone establishes that a selected panel represents persistent dissent under the shifted policy.
Could we call attrition session noise?

No. Session noise is variation in annotations from observed sessions; attrition is a lack of an observation from someone who does not participate in a later session. Treating missing feedback as though it were a noisy annotation would conflate the two sources of uncertainty the question needs to keep apart.
Does knowing that attrition depends on policy outputs tell us its precise mechanism?

No. It states a dependence that must be taken seriously, but does not specify which outputs affect recontact, how strongly, or how that dependence interacts with preferences and session noise. Supplying a particular mechanism as fact would go beyond the question.
Would measuring session consistency among returners let us infer consistency among those who left?

Not without a justified bridge between the observed returners and the missing participants. Consistency among returners concerns their observed responses. Output-dependent attrition means that extending it to those who left may be especially difficult, because their absence could be related to the outputs about which one wants to learn.
What if someone treats pseudonymous recontact as equivalent to observing group identity?

That would conflate a way of linking a participant's observations with knowing their annotator group. PanelDRO-RLHF proposes pseudonymous linkage, not observed group identities. A persistence argument could use the former without claiming the latter, and a group-level performance conclusion would require its own basis.
Does the question say that attrition has already biased a measured win rate?

No. It asks whether output-dependent attrition limits our ability to distinguish persistent dissent from session noise. It gives no measured attrition rate, recovery result, or win-rate effect. An explanation for a particular performance outcome would be an additional claim.
Could we treat an answer based only on observed responses as an answer to the whole question?

Only if its scope is stated clearly. An analysis of observed, recontacted participants might address persistence in that selected set. The question is harder because policy-output-dependent attrition may prevent extending that interpretation to missing respondents or the full feedback population. A complete answer would have to confront that limit rather than ignore it.
Is there a concise way to pose the issue without assuming it can or cannot be resolved?

Yes: 'Under what conditions do pseudonymous cross-policy recontact and randomized repeated comparisons distinguish persistent dissent from session noise when the likelihood of recontact depends on policy outputs?' That preserves the proposal's tools, the output-dependent attrition, and the uncertainty about identifiability.
And what is the shortest careful response to the original question?

Not necessarily. Cross-policy recontact and randomized repetitions can inform the distinction for observed feedback, but output-dependent annotator attrition can make persistent dissent, session noise, and selection difficult to disentangle. Whether they can be separated requires explicit identifiability conditions; the question alone does not establish them.

Here is a hypothesis for PanelDRO-RLHF: with at least 15% recontact per history stratum and independent three-view repeats, PanelDRO identifies dissent; attrition that depends on unobserved preferences remains nonidentifiable. How should we state that carefully?

State both the proposed positive condition and its limit as a hypothesis: if recontact reaches ≥15% in each history stratum and the three-view repeats are independent, PanelDRO can identify persistent dissent separately from session noise. The proposed boundary is that attrition depending on unobserved preferences remains nonidentifiable. Neither the sufficiency of the 15% threshold nor the applicability of the independence assumption has been established by stating the hypothesis.
Why is it important to say 'per history stratum' instead of just '15% recontact'?

Because the threshold is conditional on each history stratum. An overall recontact rate of ≥15% could coexist with a lower rate in a particular stratum and would not satisfy the stated condition. The hypothesis does not specify how the strata are defined or how many there are, so those details should not be filled in.
Is the condition strictly greater than 15%?
No. The symbol ≥ means at least 15%, including 15% itself. It is a proposed lower bound on recontact in each history stratum, not an exact rate or a requirement to exceed 15% strictly.
Does that threshold say how many individual annotators must be recontacted?
No. A percentage per stratum cannot be converted to a count without knowing the size and definition of each stratum. The hypothesis supplies neither those sizes nor a total recontact count.
What work are the independent three-view repeats meant to do?

They are the proposed repeated observations used to distinguish a recurring preference pattern from variation associated with a session. Independence is important because three linked errors would not provide the same information as three independent views. The hypothesis does not specify the exact comparisons repeated or the process used to make the views independent.
Can we infer independence just because three comparisons were recorded?

No. 'Three-view' specifies a repeated-view structure, while 'independent' adds a separate assumption about those repeats. Counting three observations does not establish independence if their variations are linked. Both parts must remain in the hypothesis's conditions.
Does three-view mean recontacting the same participant three times across policies?

Not necessarily. The hypothesis names independent three-view repeats and ≥15% recontact per history stratum, but does not specify how many recontacts each participant has or how the repeats are arranged across policies. It would be an added implementation detail to equate the three views with three cross-policy recontacts.
When we say PanelDRO 'identifies dissent,' what should that refer to?

In this setting it refers to distinguishing a persistent dissenting preference pattern from session noise using the proposed linked and repeated feedback. It should not mean declaring every conflicting annotation to be stable dissent. It also should not be expanded into a claim that annotator group identities have been observed or recovered.
Could a pseudonymous link count as an observed group identity?

No. Pseudonymous cross-policy recontact links feedback without supplying an annotator's group identity. A link may help examine persistence in responses, but it does not itself say which group someone belongs to. The hypothesis is about identifying dissent, not naming groups.
Does the hypothesis answer the question about attrition depending on policy outputs?

It proposes a conditional answer, but its boundary must be kept clear. Recontact of ≥15% per history stratum and independent three-view repeats are proposed conditions for identifying dissent. Separately, it says attrition depending on unobserved preferences remains nonidentifiable. Dependence on policy outputs and dependence on unobserved preferences should not be treated as interchangeable: the hypothesis does not say that every form of output-dependent attrition is harmless.
What is the difference between those two kinds of dependence?

Policy outputs concern what the policy presents; an unobserved preference is information about what an annotator would prefer that is not available in the observations. Attrition could depend on policy outputs without the hypothesis specifying all the resulting selection effects. Its explicit nonidentifiability limit concerns dependence on unobserved preferences, which can leave missing responses systematically related to the very dissent one wants to identify.
Could we claim that 15% recontact completely corrects output-dependent attrition?

No. The hypothesis does not say that recontact at the proposed threshold corrects every selection effect. Its positive claim is about identifying dissent under the stated recontact and independent-repeat conditions, and its negative claim flags a form of attrition that remains nonidentifiable. A blanket correction claim would exceed both.
Why would dependence on an unobserved preference be particularly difficult?

If whether someone returns depends on a preference that is not observed for the missing response, the available feedback may not tell us what the nonreturners would have said. A pattern among those recontacted could then be consistent with different patterns among those absent. That is the intuition behind the hypothesis's nonidentifiability boundary, not a newly established proof of it.
If each history stratum meets the 15% threshold, doesn't that cover the missing-preference problem too?

Not under this hypothesis. Meeting a recontact percentage within every history stratum says how much feedback is observed by that grouping; it does not reveal preferences that affect attrition but remain unobserved. The hypothesis expressly says unobserved-preference-dependent attrition remains nonidentifiable despite stating its positive recontact and repetition conditions.
So 'remains nonidentifiable' doesn't mean no response can be interpreted at all?

Correct. It is a limit on the intended identification of dissent in the presence of that form of attrition, not a claim that observed responses contain no information. One could still describe observed feedback. The issue is whether it uniquely supports the broader distinction between persistent dissent and session noise when missingness depends on unobserved preferences.
Would repeated agreement among recontacted people overcome that limit?

Repeated agreement can inform an assessment of the people and comparisons actually observed, especially under the independence premise. It does not supply the unobserved preferences of people whose attrition depends on those preferences. The nonidentifiability clause warns against extending a pattern among returners to the missing feedback without further justification.
Can I call 15% a proven minimum necessary for identification?

No. The hypothesis proposes sufficiency at ≥15% recontact per history stratum together with independent three-view repeats. It does not establish the claim yet, and it does not say that lower recontact rates can never suffice under other conditions. A proposed lower-bound condition is not a proved universal necessity threshold.
Does it also specify a flip-noise rate or an anchor-overlap percentage?

No. This hypothesis specifies a recontact threshold per history stratum, independent three-view repeats, and the nonidentifiability limit for unobserved-preference-dependent attrition. It gives no flip-noise percentage or anchor-overlap threshold. Adding either would change its stated conditions.
What if I say it proves PanelDRO-RLHF's pessimistic latent-profile objective improves worst-group wins?

That would conflate identification with policy performance. This hypothesis concerns when PanelDRO can identify dissent and when attrition leaves it nonidentifiable. It reports no latent-profile win rate, worst-group preference win rate, comparison to pooled RLHF, or feedback-budget-matched performance result.
Would the positive and negative parts contradict each other?

Not if their scopes are stated explicitly. The positive part proposes identification under the specified recontact and independent-repeat conditions. The negative part marks unobserved-preference-dependent attrition as a case in which identification remains unavailable. An eventual formal statement would have to spell out how the positive conditions exclude or otherwise handle that limiting case; the hypothesis should not imply that the recontact threshold overrides it.
Can you give me a compact formulation with the limitation in the same sentence?

Hypothesis: with ≥15% pseudonymous cross-policy recontact in each history stratum and independent three-view repeats, PanelDRO-RLHF can identify persistent dissent separately from session noise, but dissent remains nonidentifiable when attrition depends on unobserved preferences. Both the proposed sufficiency and its precise limits remain to be established.

For PanelDRO-RLHF, let's use PanelAttrition-Sim to test three-view dissent recovery with at least 15% history-stratified recontact, and construct observationally equivalent preference-dependent-attrition counterexamples. Can we unpack the activity?

It has two parts. In PanelAttrition-Sim, examine whether PanelDRO recovers dissent using three-view observations when recontact is ≥15% within each history stratum. Separately, construct counterexamples in which preference-dependent attrition permits different underlying accounts to produce the same observations. The simulation test and the counterexamples address different sides of the identification question; this activity does not report either one's outcome.
What exactly is being tested in the simulation?

The specified target is PanelDRO’s three-view dissent recovery under the stated recontact condition. In other words, the activity asks whether the observations support recovering a persistent dissenting preference pattern rather than merely fitting variation in the annotations. It does not specify a recovery metric, an error value, or a success threshold for that recovery.
Is ≥15% a rate across everyone who might be recontacted?

No. The qualifier is history-stratified: recontact must reach at least 15% within each history stratum. An overall rate of 15% or more would not establish that condition if a particular stratum fell below it. The activity does not define the strata or give their sizes.
Does exactly 15% satisfy the recontact condition?
Yes. ≥15% includes 15% itself. The activity does not require a rate strictly above 15%, nor does it say that every stratum must have the same rate once the lower bound is met.
Could I translate that percentage into a number of recontacted annotators?
Not without the number of annotators in each history stratum. No stratum sizes or total participant count are provided, so the activity should retain the percentage rather than invent a count.
Do the three views mean three separate history strata?

No. Three-view describes the repeated-observation structure used to examine dissent recovery; history strata describe how the recontact condition is applied. They are separate aspects of the activity. Neither the number of strata nor a particular arrangement of repeated comparisons is specified.
Should the three views be called independent?

The identifiability hypothesis being examined includes independent three-view repeats. This activity calls for testing three-view dissent recovery, but does not itself describe how independence is implemented or verified in PanelAttrition-Sim. It would be reasonable to keep that premise visible when interpreting a test of the hypothesis, without saying independence has already been established by the simulation's name or by counting three views.
Can I say the simulation establishes that 15% recontact is sufficient to identify dissent?

Not before any result is given, and a simulation result alone would need its scope stated carefully. The activity is to test recovery in PanelAttrition-Sim under ≥15% recontact per history stratum. A general sufficiency claim about identification would require explicit assumptions and an argument; the planned test is not itself that argument.
What does 'dissent recovery' mean without assuming annotator group identities are observed?

It concerns recovering a stable preference pattern that conflicts with another pattern, not attaching a known group label to the people expressing it. PanelDRO's proposed cross-policy links are pseudonymous, and the activity does not call for observed annotator group identities as an input. Recovering a dissenting pattern should not be restated as identifying a named group.
Does pseudonymous recontact mean we can tell whether the same participant responds across policy settings?

That is the role of the proposed pseudonymous cross-policy link: relating feedback across policies without treating a participant's group identity as observed. The activity does not specify a recontact protocol or guarantee that every participant returns. Its ≥15% condition is stated per history stratum precisely as a condition on the feedback that is recontacted.
How does session noise fit into this activity?

It is the alternative to persistent dissent that the three-view recovery question is meant to help distinguish. Variation in responses from one session need not represent a stable conflicting preference. The activity proposes examining recovery under repeated views, but it does not define a particular noise distribution or report that session noise has been separated successfully.
Could I say every repeated disagreement in PanelAttrition-Sim must be stable dissent?

No. The purpose of testing dissent recovery is to find out whether the available observations distinguish stable dissent from variation in annotations. Merely seeing disagreement, even repeatedly, does not make its interpretation automatic. Attrition adds another reason to be careful about what the observed feedback represents.
Now, what makes the proposed counterexamples 'observationally equivalent'?

Observational equivalence means that different underlying accounts give the same observable feedback, so the observed data alone cannot distinguish them. In this activity, the counterexamples are to use preference-dependent attrition to expose such an ambiguity. That explains what the constructions must demonstrate without inventing their specific preferences, response rates, or comparisons.
Why is preference-dependent attrition important to those examples?

Because if participation depends on preferences that are unavailable for people who do not respond, the observed panel may omit precisely the feedback needed to distinguish underlying accounts. The counterexamples would make that limitation concrete by exhibiting indistinguishable observations despite a relevant underlying difference. The activity calls for constructing them; it does not yet supply a construction.
Does 'preference-dependent' mean that policy outputs have no role in attrition?

No such exclusion is stated. The current activity specifies preference-dependent attrition for the counterexamples. It does not supply a full model of how preferences and policy outputs might jointly affect recontact. We should not turn the counterexample description into an assertion that attrition depends on preferences alone.
If we meet ≥15% recontact in every history stratum, could the preference-dependent counterexamples still matter?

Yes. A positive recontact rate within each stratum does not, on its own, reveal the preferences of those who did not return. The activity does not yet report the details or conclusions of such constructions.
Would three views necessarily remove the observational equivalence?

Are the counterexamples just unusual simulation runs?

Could a strong recovery result in the simulation invalidate the counterexamples?

Not necessarily. Good recovery in a particular simulated setting would concern that setting. An observational-equivalence counterexample would concern a setting in which the observations cannot distinguish two underlying accounts. Both could be relevant to describing the conditions and limits of identification; neither result is reported by this activity.
And would one counterexample mean recontact is useless in every setting?

No. A counterexample would establish a limitation for the conditions it constructs, not that pseudonymous recontact or three-view repeats provide no information in any setting. The activity tests recovery under a specified recontact condition while also examining a possible nonidentifiability boundary.
Should we use the counterexamples to claim exactly how many views would be necessary?

Not from the activity as stated. It names three-view recovery and observationally equivalent preference-dependent-attrition counterexamples. It does not call for comparing every possible number of views or proving a universal minimum view count.

Not directly in its stated measurements. What should we avoid claiming about the counterexamples before constructing them?

Avoid describing a particular pair of preference patterns, a particular attrition mechanism, or an observed-data distribution as though it has already been constructed. Also avoid declaring a blanket impossibility result for all forms of attrition. The stated task is to construct observationally equivalent counterexamples specifically involving preference-dependent attrition.

It would distinguish the ≥15% *per-history-stratum* recontact condition from an aggregate rate; three-view recovery of stable dissent from group-identity recovery; simulation behavior from a general identifiability claim; and an observational-equivalence counterexample from a merely poor recovery score. Those distinctions preserve what each part is intended to examine without predetermining either outcome.

PanelAttrition-Sim found that, despite 18% history-stratified recontact, three independent rank-deficient views left dissent unidentifiable even under history-conditional attrition. How should we report that?

Does it mean PanelDRO produced no useful observations at all?

How should I read the 18% recontact figure?

Would raising the recontact percentage necessarily identify dissent?

Is 18% supposed to be a failure threshold?

What does 'even under history-conditional attrition' add?

So it wouldn't be accurate to say this finding depends on attrition selecting on unobserved preferences?

Could I instead say that history-conditional attrition always prevents identification?

And it doesn't mean all output-dependent attrition is the same as history-conditional attrition?

Right. This evidence names history-conditional attrition. It does not characterize every way attrition might depend on policy outputs or equate all those cases with the one studied. The safest account retains the precise attrition qualification given.

No. 'Unidentifiable' means the observations did not establish the distinction at issue; it does not mean that no persistent dissent existed. The evidence should not be turned into a substantive finding about whether any annotators held a conflicting preference.
Does the result show that observed disagreement was definitely session noise?

No. If dissent is unidentifiable, the feedback does not warrant declaring the conflicting observations to be persistent dissent *or* declaring them to be session noise on that basis alone. The finding concerns inability to distinguish the interpretations under the reported conditions.

Should we call it a worst-group performance failure?

Does this evidence tell us anything about optimizing pessimistic latent-profile win rates?

The supplied finding states that dissent was unidentifiable under the specified conditions. It does not give a particular pair of observationally equivalent constructions or their details. The 18% history-stratified recontact did not settle identifiability in PanelAttrition-Sim: dissent remained unidentifiable with three independent rank-deficient views, even under history-conditional attrition. What is the difference between the two attrition conditions?

What exactly should 'remained nonidentifiable' convey?
